item.title: 3D Surface Matching Based on Adaptive Threshold and Curvature Map
item.description:
The problem

In industrial defect inspection and robotic sorting, a 3D scanner has a limited acquisition range, so each scan gives a single point cloud or depth map from one viewpoint, covering only part of the surface. Matching a workpiece model against such a scan is hard: feature points are sparse, there is a lot of redundant data, and the overlap is low.

The standard tools each have a weak spot, according to the authors. ICP (iterative closest point) aligns very accurately from a good starting pose, but is sensitive to initialisation and can get stuck in a local minimum when the geometry is incomplete or ambiguous. RANSAC-based methods struggle to separate adjacent or continuous surfaces. The integral volume descriptor (IVD) makes coarse matching more robust to noise, but its cost grows quickly on dense or noisy clouds. Learning-based registration, in turn, typically needs large annotated datasets and heavy computation, and generalises poorly across industrial scenes. This paper aims at a geometric method that keeps only the points that matter, so that IVD and ICP have less to process.

How it works

The method targets workpieces with pronounced curvature. It first shrinks the model point cloud to its high-curvature points, with a threshold that it finds by itself, and then matches in two stages: a coarse pose from IVD correspondences, and a fine pose from ICP.

  1. Depth map and curvature map. The model point cloud is converted into a depth map. For each pixel, a quadratic surface is fitted to its neighbourhood, and the resulting average curvature becomes the pixel value of the surface curvature map.
  2. Adaptive threshold iteration. From the histogram of curvature values (bin width by Scott’s rule), the method fixes a target share of high-curvature points: the points above an upper percentile. The threshold is β = μ + Kσ, with the mean μ and standard deviation σ of the curvature map. If the share of points above the threshold is too large, K is increased by 1%; if too small, decreased by 1%. This repeats until the share lies within a tolerance of the target. The points above the final threshold are the model point cloud used for matching.
  3. IVD correspondences. The IVD of a point is the volume where a sphere around it overlaps the inside of the surface; it is computed by convolving a voxel occupancy grid with a spherical grid, which avoids the noise sensitivity of differential features. Model points and scene points with similar IVD and position give preliminary point pairs.
  4. Coarse pose by SVD. After removing the centroids of both point sets, the covariance matrix of the pairs is decomposed by SVD, giving the approximate pose of the target in the scene.
  5. Fine matching by ICP. The model is moved by the coarse pose, and ICP then minimises the squared distances to the scene points, stopping when the objective changes by less than a set value.

Results

Lowest RMSE of the compared methods on both workpieces: 0.681 on Workpiece 1 and 0.405 on Workpiece 2, against 1.194 and 0.521 for IVD-SVD+ICP without feature selection (Table III).
The thresholds adapt per model, so no manual tuning is needed: the converged K was 0.405, 0.605 and 0.368 for the three models (Table II).
Under added Gaussian noise (std 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) the RMSE stays below IVD-SVD+ICP in every case, for example 0.826 against 1.01 at std 0.3 on Workpiece 1 (Table IV).

The experiments use point clouds from a structured-light camera of two workpieces (Fig. 4 of the paper). Workpiece 1 is matched with two models, front and back, in a scene of 149,469 points; Workpiece 2 uses one model (Table I). Accuracy is measured by RMSE between matched points, averaged over all targets when the scene holds several.

The segmentation takes the top 20% of curvature values as the target (80th percentile). The segmented clouds are much sparser than the originals, yet the edges and other geometrically significant points remain. Table II lists the converged parameters: the three models needed 502, 904 and 622 iterations and ended with 3,671, 3,369 and 4,860 feature points.

For matching, the paper compares IVD-SVD+ICP, the same pipeline with the threshold set by hand through three fixed K values (0.3, 0.6, 0.9), and the proposed method. The proposed method has the lowest RMSE on both workpieces. The margin is small on Workpiece 2, where K = 0.3 reaches 0.406 against 0.405. The fixed-K runs show how much the choice of K matters on Workpiece 1: RMSE ranged from 0.752 to 0.991, whereas the adaptive threshold needs no such tuning. Running time (Table III) is in the same range: 543 ms and 337 ms for the proposed method, against 532 ms and 489 ms for IVD-SVD+ICP, and some fixed-K variants were faster on Workpiece 2.

To test noise robustness, Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 was added to the point clouds, as low, medium and high noise, and the method was compared with IVD-SVD+ICP. The proposed method’s RMSE grows with noise but stays lower in all six cases: 0.748, 0.826 and 0.978 on Workpiece 1 (against 0.811, 1.01 and 1.121), and 0.417, 0.497 and 0.557 on Workpiece 2 (against 0.656, 0.667 and 0.728) (Tables IV and V). In low and medium noise, the matching shows no positional deviation. The authors state that the method still has limitations on high-noise point clouds, and name further work on feature extraction, more data for cross-scenario validation, and error analysis for heterogeneous point clouds.

item.title: Learning-based reconstruction of moving transparent objects
item.description:
The problem

Transparent moving objects have long been challenging targets in optical imaging: they have high transmittance and weak texture, and their imaging involves both refraction and reflection. Unlike conventional opaque rigid objects, a transparent object reflects the fringe patterns projected by phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) from both its front and rear surfaces, so the captured images show severe fringe superposition. When the object moves, its refraction effects are further coupled with motion-induced errors, which makes accurate reconstruction significantly harder.

How it works

The paper systematically analyzes how the imaging mechanisms of transparent objects influence geometric modeling and motion estimation, and proposes a learning-based reconstruction method for moving transparent objects that works in two stages.

  1. Superimposed fringes. PSP fringe patterns are reflected by both the front and rear surfaces of the moving transparent object and overlap in the captured images.
  2. Fringe separation. A diffusion model separates the superimposed fringe patterns.
  3. Reconstruction of the moving object. The moving object is then reconstructed based on the SIFT algorithm and two-dimensional motion equations.

Results

Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in complex dynamic transparent scenarios.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1117/12.3111340.

item.title: Self-calibrating structured light three-dimensional imaging method with fringe projection
item.description:
The problem

Industrial inspection asks for 3D measurement that is efficient, economical and highly precise, and structured-light 3D measurement meets these requirements. In a monocular camera–projector system that reconstructs surfaces by phase-shifting fringe projection, long-term operational stability is the key bottleneck for measurement accuracy: external factors such as vibration make the system’s extrinsic parameters move slowly, which weakens the triangulation constraints and lowers the accuracy of the measurement results.

How it works

The paper develops a self-calibrating fringe-projection 3D imaging technique that integrates bundle adjustment. The surface of the object being reconstructed becomes a constraint in the calibration itself.

  1. Drifting extrinsics. Vibration slowly moves the extrinsic parameters of the camera–projector system, weakening the triangulation constraints.
  2. Initial values. The independent calibration parameters of the camera and of the projector serve as the initial values.
  3. Joint optimisation (the bundle adjustment). The surface point cloud of the object being reconstructed is added to the optimisation as a constraint, giving a collaborative optimisation model of the camera parameters, the projector parameters and the scene’s 3D points.
  4. Corrected extrinsics. With this model the system’s extrinsic parameters are corrected rapidly and accurately.

Results

In the experiments, the technique significantly reduces the reliance on high-precision targets and strict flatness requirements without interrupting the measurement process, and cuts the cost of manual intervention and operation while ensuring reconstruction accuracy and measurement efficiency.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1117/12.3114025.

item.title: SuP: Sub-cloud Driven Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two 3D scans of the same scene. Modern methods do this precisely when the two scans share a lot of geometry. In applications such as large-scale mapping and autonomous navigation, though, the views often share only a small part of the scene. Once the shared surface falls below about 30 %, classic ICP and learned methods alike struggle to find reliable correspondences, and registration slows, drifts or fails.

The paper traces these failures to the regions that are not shared: they can still be geometrically or semantically similar to each other, and matching the two whole clouds then produces wrong correspondences that obscure the correct ones. Earlier work tried to predict which points lie in the overlap, but that prediction depends on consistent features and becomes less effective on low-overlap pairs. Later methods strengthen the features with attention, geometric encodings, semantics or colour, yet their accuracy still drops as overlap falls.

How it works

SuP changes what it looks for. Two scans may overlap only a little overall, but if each is cut into smaller pieces and the pieces are matched pairwise, a subset of these sub-cloud pairs has high overlap. SuP calls these high-overlap pairs anchor pairs. It finds them in two phases, then builds its matches only from inside them.

  1. Features for the whole scan. A KPConv backbone extracts point features at several scales, and attention layers exchange context within and between the two scans. By default SuP uses the colour-enhanced backbone and attention of ColorPCR.
  2. Subdivide. Each scan is split into k sub-clouds. Farthest point sampling picks well-spread centroids, and each sub-cloud collects a centroid’s nearest neighbours within a radius.
  3. Phase I: overlap-guided prior weighting (OPS). For every source–target pair of sub-clouds, SuP measures how strongly their point features agree, counting only mutual top-ranked correlations, and keeps the best-scoring pairs as candidates. This is an efficient first filter against pairs that do not overlap.
  4. Phase II: multi-scale post-weighting (MPN). Each candidate pair is aligned with a preliminary pose from a weighted SVD. A small learned network then checks whether points that now sit close together also have similar features, at two scales. The pairs with the highest feature-consensus weights become anchor pairs. During training, the network is supervised by how well each candidate actually aligns (an alignment-aware weighting loss).
  5. Merge-to-match. Inlier correspondences from all anchor pairs are merged, refined on the denser points, and passed to a standard estimator (RANSAC or the RANSAC-free LGR) to compute the final rotation and translation.

In the reported setup, each scan is cut into 6 sub-clouds, giving 36 possible pairs. OPS keeps 24 of them, and the top 8 by feature consensus become anchor pairs.

Results

Registration recall 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch with the RANSAC-free LGR estimator, the highest among the methods compared with LGR (Table 2).
98.1 % and 90.4 % with RANSAC, and the highest registration recall at every sampling level from 5,000 down to 250 correspondences (Table 1).
Lowest pose errors: 1.374° / 0.046 m on Color3DMatch and 2.493° / 0.074 m on Color3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The evaluation uses colour-enhanced versions of the indoor 3DMatch benchmark: Color3DMatch, with pairs overlapping by more than 30 %, and Color3DLoMatch, the harder split with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of scan pairs aligned to within 0.2 m RMSE. SuP uses ColorPCR’s colour-enhanced backbone by default; compared with ColorPCR alone, the strongest baseline, it raises recall from 96.5 % to 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and from 88.3 % to 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch under LGR. The share of correct matches rises as well: with 250 sampled correspondences on Color3DLoMatch, 76.0 % of SuP’s matches are correct (inlier ratio), against 68.0 % for ColorPCR.

The sub-cloud step also works as an add-on to other methods. Added to GeoTransformer, it raises Color3DLoMatch recall from 74.0 % to 76.7 %; added to PEAL, from 81.2 % to 83.4 % (Table 4). In the ablation study, adding the four components one at a time (OPS, the feature-consensus weights, MPN and the alignment-aware loss) raises recall at every step on both benchmarks (Table 5). Sub-cloud size matters as well: smaller sub-clouds may lower recall because of insufficient overlap, larger ones miss local detail, and the default radius setting τ = 0.35 gives the best balance (Table 6). The paper’s limitation section notes that features from scans captured with very different sensors could weaken OPS and MPN, and suggests feature normalisation or domain adaptation as a next step.

item.title: A Reversible Grayscale Method Based on Bit-Field Multi-Channel Fusion Encoding
item.description:
The problem

Grayscale images are widely used because they cut computational complexity, storage and transmission cost. In many applications, though, the original colours are needed again later, so the conversion should be reversible: the grayscale image has to carry enough colour information to restore the RGB image.

Traditional reversible grayscale methods, such as histogram shifting and wavelet-packet data hiding, embed colour cues into the luminance channel. They usually impose extra transform-domain constraints or need several auxiliary channels, which adds computation and memory. Deep-learning methods reach high reconstruction fidelity but bring high inference latency, large models, limited interpretability and a strong dependence on training data.

How it works

The method needs no training. Each RGB pixel is converted to the HSV colour space, which separates the chromatic part (hue H, saturation S) from the luminance part (value V). The three components are quantized to a, b and c bits with a + b + c = 16 and written side by side into the bit fields (H in the high bits, V in the low bits) of one 16-bit grayscale pixel. Decoding reads the fields back with shifts and masks. The whole pipeline uses only quantization and bitwise operations, and it is exactly invertible except for the quantization error.

  1. Normalize. The three channels of an 8-bit RGB pixel are divided by 255, so they lie in [0, 1].
  2. RGB to HSV. The standard conversion gives hue H as an angle from 0° to 360°, saturation S and value V; H is then scaled to [0, 1).
  3. Allocate the 16 bits. The output pixel’s 16 bits are split into a bits for H, b for S and c for V. The split can follow the image statistics, with a and b proportional to the variances of H and S and c taking the rest. The paper also gives four example schemes; the balanced Scheme 1 uses (6, 4, 6).
  4. Quantize and pack. H, S and V pass through a non-linear (gamma) mapping that favours perceptually sensitive ranges, are quantized to 2a, 2b and 2c levels, and are packed as IG = (Hq ≪ (b + c)) | (Sq ≪ c) | Vq. The result is a single-channel 16-bit grayscale image.
  5. Decode. Bit masks and shifts recover Hq, Sq and Vq; inverse quantization and the standard HSV-to-RGB transform give the 8-bit RGB pixel back.

The choice of (a, b, c) trades accuracy between the channels. Because people are sensitive to hue changes, the authors recommend a ≥ 5 (32 hue levels) to avoid visible colour shifts, and c ≥ 6 (64 value levels) to prevent banding; b can be reduced for images with little colour. Hue is circular, so a non-linear quantization keeps errors small near 0°/360°, and Floyd–Steinberg error diffusion spreads the remaining quantization error spatially.

Results

Encoding 3.71 ms and decoding 7.01 ms per Kodak image with Scheme 1, against 175.30 / 125.24 ms for IDN and 2486.75 / 2453.82 ms for the CNN-based method (Table II).
PSNR 34.80 dB, SSIM 0.9726 on Kodak with Scheme 1; higher is better, and PSNR is below IDN (42.16 dB) and the CNN-based method (37.40 dB) (Table II).
PSNR 34.06 / 34.48 / 32.20 dB on Urban100 / BSD500 / McMaster with Scheme 1, with encoding and decoding times between 2.80 and 3.82 ms (Table III).

The method was evaluated on four datasets: Kodak PhotoCD (24 images), Urban100 (100 urban scenes), BSD500 (500 natural landscapes) and McMaster (18 images). It was compared with two learning-based invertible grayscale methods, IDN and a CNN-based method, using MAE, PSNR, SSIM, FSIM and LPIPS, and timed on an AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060. Of the four bit-allocation schemes, Scheme 1 (6, 4, 6) gives the best balance; Scheme 2 (5, 5, 6) reaches the highest SSIM of the four on Kodak (0.9779), and Scheme 4 (6, 5, 5) is the fastest at 3.21 ms encoding and 4.49 ms decoding. The 16-bit files are also slightly smaller on Kodak: 633.20 KB for Scheme 1, against 721.47 KB for IDN and 660.87 KB for the CNN-based method (Table II).

The speed comes at a cost in fidelity. On Kodak, IDN reaches 42.16 dB PSNR and the CNN-based method 37.40 dB, against 34.80 dB here, and the authors note that a recent reversible data-hiding method reports 43.69 dB. They see the method as a lightweight, interpretable alternative for resource-constrained settings such as edge and embedded systems, and plan adaptive allocation algorithms and reversible compression to close the quality gap, and FPGA/ASIC implementations to further cut latency.

item.title: FPD: Fringe Photometric Deflectometry when Fringe Meets Photometric Stereo
item.description:
The problem

Many industrial parts are neither purely matte nor purely mirror-like. The back of a phone, for example, has a glossy logo on a surface whose specular reflection is weaker, and defects such as scratches and fingerprint smudges have to be found on both. Two established optical methods each cover only half of this. Photometric stereo (PS) recovers surface normals from images taken under several illumination directions; it works well on diffuse (Lambertian) regions but degrades where specular highlights appear. Phase Measuring Deflectometry (PMD) measures surface gradients from the reflection of sinusoidal fringes; it is accurate on specular surfaces but unreliable on matte areas, where fringe contrast is low.

As a result, existing inspection methods often fail to detect subtle defects when specular highlights or diffuse textures dominate. Few earlier works merge the two methods: one combined photogrammetry with PS, another fused line-structured light with PS but had difficulties in highly reflective areas.

How it works

FPD captures the data for both methods in one cycle, runs a PMD branch and a PS branch, and fuses their outputs pixel by pixel. The PMD branch also measures how specular each pixel is, and that measurement sets the fusion weights.

  1. One capture cycle. A projector displays three kinds of patterns: binary patterns that simulate four-quadrant illumination for PS, and horizontal (fringe-x) and vertical (fringe-y) sinusoidal fringes for PMD. The camera records 12 images per cycle.
  2. PMD branch. With four phase-shifted fringe images per pixel, the mean intensity is A, the specular component S is computed from the fringe modulation, and the diffuse component is D = A − S; glossiness is S / A. Multi-frequency unwrapping gives the absolute phase, whose x and y derivatives form the phase gradient magnitude P.
  3. PS branch. The four binary-pattern images, using the PMD specular and diffuse reflection maps as prior information, form an intensity matrix of images × pixels. Its singular value decomposition gives the surface normals, from which the surface gradients and the mean curvature H are computed, with CUDA acceleration.
  4. Weights from reflectance. Each pixel gets wPMD = S / (S + D) and wPS = D / (S + D). Glossy pixels lean on PMD, more diffuse pixels on PS, and the transition between them is smooth.
  5. Fusion. The result is R = wPMD·P + wPS·H. PMD dominates where fringes are reliable, PS where fine diffuse detail needs to be kept.

Results

Scratch on the glossy logo: missed by the PS mean curvature map, kept by PMD and by FPD (Fig. 4).
Fingerprint smudge outside the logo: missed by the PMD phase gradient map, kept by PS and by FPD (Fig. 4).
Defect detection in Smart3 (a commercial inspection software): PS-based detection fails on the strongly specular region, PMD-based detection fails where reflection is weaker, and the FPD result supports detecting both (Fig. 7).

The test object is the back of an iPhone, which shows both diffuse and specular reflection. It was imaged on a platform with a projector, a camera and mounting structures, with a 12-image cycle of binary, fringe-x and fringe-y patterns, and processed on a PC with an Intel Core i5-13500 CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. The comparison is between the three reconstructed maps of the same capture: the PS mean curvature map, the PMD phase gradient map and the FPD fusion result, which the authors find more complete and consistent across both types of feature. Defect detection was then run on each of the three maps with Smart3, a commercial inspection software from OPT Machine Vision: scratch detection, and smudge detection by line extraction. FPD has also been integrated into commercial defect inspection software.

The authors name calibration of the integrated system and height measurement for complex surfaces as future work.

item.title: GCMA6D: Graph Convolution and Cross-Modality Attention Fusion for 6D Pose Estimation
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers the 3D rotation and translation of an object relative to the camera, a step that robotic manipulation and augmented reality depend on. It remains hard for low-texture objects and under partial occlusion. Methods that use RGB images alone lack depth information, which limits their robustness in complex environments. RGB-D methods such as DenseFusion fuse colour and point-cloud features pixel by pixel, but they describe the geometry with PointNet, which may miss fine local detail. Methods that add local feature modelling, such as PVN3D, raise the computational cost, and the size and inference latency of large foundation models hinder real-time deployment.

GCMA6D builds on the pixel-wise fusion of DenseFusion, the baseline of its ablation study, and strengthens each part of it: graph convolution models local geometry, Large Kernel Attention sharpens the image features, and a cross-modality attention module lets colour and geometry inform each other before they are fused.

How it works

The network takes a single RGB-D image. It segments the object, extracts colour features from the image crop and geometric features from the object’s point cloud, fuses them with attention, and regresses the pose from every pixel of the object.

  1. Segment and crop. The semantic segmentation network from PoseCNN produces a mask for each object. The mask crops the colour image and cuts the object out of the depth map, which the camera intrinsics convert into a 3D point cloud. This suppresses background interference before any features are computed.
  2. Colour features with Large Kernel Attention. A ResNet18 backbone and a pyramid pooling module extract multi-scale features from the image crop. Large Kernel Attention, a depth-wise convolution, a depth-wise dilated convolution and a 1×1 convolution, builds an attention map that is multiplied with the features, so the network captures local texture and edges as well as longer-range context.
  3. Geometric features with 3DGCN and PointNet. A 3D graph convolutional network applies learnable 3D graph-convolution kernels to the neighbourhood of each point, followed by graph max pooling, to model local geometric structure. A PointNet branch processes the points with fully connected layers and obtains a global shape feature through max pooling.
  4. Cross-modality attention. The CMA-Net module takes the colour features (F1), the 3DGCN features (F2) and the PointNet features (F3). One dot-product attention uses F1, F2, F3 as query, key and value to enhance the colour features; a second uses F2, F1, F3 to enhance the point features. A Squeeze-and-Excitation module reweights the channels of both outputs and of F3, and the three are concatenated.
  5. Dense fusion and pose. The fused features of each pixel pass through shared MLPs and average pooling to form a global feature, which is appended to every pixel’s feature. Each pixel then predicts a rotation, a translation and a confidence; the most confident prediction is kept. Following DenseFusion, a small network then refines it iteratively by predicting residual poses.

Results

97.7 % mean accuracy on LineMOD (ADD(-S) within 10 % of the object diameter), against 94.3 % for DenseFusion (Table 2).
Each module alone improves on the 94.3 % baseline: graph convolution (3DGCN) 96.9 %, Large Kernel Attention (LKA) 96.2 %, cross-modality attention (CMA-Net) 95.4 % (Table 1).
92.9 % AUC (area under the ADD(-S) accuracy curve up to 10 cm) and 95.7 % of poses under 2 cm on YCB-Video, against 91.2 % and 95.3 % for DenseFusion (Section 4.4).

The evaluation uses two public datasets. LineMOD contains low-texture objects against complex backgrounds under varying illumination; 15 % of the images are used for training and 85 % for testing, and a pose counts as correct when its ADD distance (ADD-S for symmetric objects) is below 10 % of the object’s diameter. In Table 2, GCMA6D has the highest mean accuracy of the seven methods compared, ahead of TMFNet (96.8 %) and QaQ (95.3 %), and reaches 100 % on the symmetric eggbox and glue. The ablation study on LineMOD shows that the modules complement each other: any two together score 96.8–97.4 %, and all three give 97.7 %.

YCB-Video has 21 objects with varying levels of occlusion; testing uses 2,949 key frames from 12 videos. Accuracy is measured as the area under the ADD(-S) accuracy curve for thresholds up to 10 cm, and as the share of poses with an error below 2 cm. GCMA6D’s 92.9 % AUC is above SaMfNet (92.6 %), G2L-Net (92.4 %), MSCNet (91.5 %) and DenseFusion (91.2 %). The authors note lower accuracy on the large and extra-large clamps: the two look very similar, so PoseCNN’s segmentation struggles to produce precise masks for them. They also name highly symmetric or heavily occluded objects as a remaining limitation, and plan to improve the processing of background-masked regions.

item.title: Photometric stereo-based defect detection for lithium battery top covers
item.description:
The problem

Cylindrical lithium batteries pick up scratches and pits on their top covers during production, from collisions, friction and other external forces. Human visual inspection is still common, but it is inefficient, inaccurate and prone to human error. Ordinary 2D machine vision lacks depth information: on a reflective metal surface it struggles in bright and dark areas, and text or dirt is easily confused with real defects. 3D methods such as structured light and fringe projection detect defects more precisely, but they are costly and data-intensive.

Photometric stereo (PS) takes a middle path. It photographs the surface under several lighting directions and recovers surface normals and curvature from the brightness changes, which makes it effective at revealing subtle surface variations. Traditional PS, however, is limited to static objects, which does not suit a production line, and very subtle defects such as shallow scratches remain hard to detect.

How it works

The method changes both the hardware and the algorithm. A line-scan camera images the cover while it moves, and a four-partition spherical integrating light source is strobed so that consecutive scan lines are lit from different directions. The usual circular opening at the top of the dome is replaced by a narrow slit, which reduces shadow artefacts. The four images are then turned into albedo and curvature maps on the GPU with CUDA, the curvature map is enhanced, and defects are extracted with image processing.

  1. Time-division acquisition. The motion platform’s encoder emits a line signal. A frequency divider produces four signals that switch the four light partitions in turn while triggering the camera, so each scan line is lit by one partition.
  2. Four images in one pass. Sorting the interleaved lines by partition gives four images of the moving cover, each under a different lighting direction.
  3. Normals by least squares. Under the Lambertian model, a pixel’s brightness is I = ρ L · N, with surface reflectance (albedo) ρ, light direction L and surface normal N. Four lights give four equations per pixel, solved by least squares. The albedo image shows foreign objects and contaminants; the normals give the surface gradients and a mean curvature image, which shows scratches, wrinkles and other defects.
  4. Enhancement. Contrast stretching widens the grey-level differences in the curvature image. A weighted least-squares filter, an edge-preserving smoother, then suppresses the texture of the workpiece while keeping defects such as scratches.
  5. Defect extraction. A region of interest is selected and the image is filtered and resampled. A difference image is formed between the original and the preprocessed (filtered and resampled) image, then thresholded; morphological operations refine the regions, and defects are kept according to their shape and grey-level features.

Results

Detection rate 95.38% for scratches and 96.43% for pits, over 376 scratches and 336 pits in 100 images of aluminium alloy surfaces with known defects (Table 2).
Sharpness 77.06 vs 16.91 and variance 168.88 vs 41.03 for the enhanced image against the method of Ren et al. (ref. 12); entropy, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity (SSIM) are also higher (Table 1).

The system runs on an industrial computer with an Intel Core i5-12500 processor and an Nvidia GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. The light direction vectors are first calibrated with a ring light, and the four images captured along these directions are processed in parallel with CUDA to produce the albedo and mean curvature images. The enhanced curvature image was compared with the method of Ren et al. on five image-quality metrics: sharpness, information entropy, variance, PSNR and SSIM (the last two are peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity). The proposed method scored higher on all five (entropy 4.70 vs 4.16, PSNR 12.37 vs 10.84, SSIM 0.527 vs 0.512), which the authors read as stronger defect contrast with the original image structure preserved. The authors also compared CPU parallel computation with Intel TBB against CUDA on the GPU over different image sizes, and found that GPU acceleration significantly improves computational efficiency.

Future work will extend the algorithm to non-Lambertian surfaces and further improve real-time processing efficiency.

item.title: SFRF6D: Selective Fewer-Reference Fusion for 6D Pose Estimation
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and 3D translation, the information a robot needs for precise grasping and assembly. Most existing methods depend on a CAD model of the object or on a large collection of reference images. Model-based methods match image features to the CAD model, which limits them in real settings where no model exists. Model-free methods such as Gen6D, OnePose and FoundationPose instead build a multi-view representation from many reference images or a video, and their cross-view alignment becomes hard to keep stable under severe occlusion or large viewpoint changes. Methods that need only a few references lose much of their matching ability when the reference views barely overlap.

SFRF6D sets out to estimate the pose with no CAD model and only a few RGB-D reference images whose poses are known, while staying robust when the object is heavily occluded.

How it works

SFRF6D first rebuilds a rough 3D shape of the object from the reference images and aligns it coarsely with the query. It then renders reference views from that coarse pose and matches them with the query through attention that is steered by 3D geometry, so that visible regions count and occluded ones do not. Finally it refines the pose and chooses among pose hypotheses by rendering and comparing.

  1. A few references, one query. The input is a small set of RGB-D reference images with ground-truth poses (four in the main experiments) and an RGB-D query image. A query mask segments the object.

  2. Coarse 3D shape. The reference view whose viewpoint is closest to the query becomes the anchor; a ResNet18 extracts its features and its depth map gives an initial object point cloud. The other references are transformed into the same world frame with their camera intrinsics and known poses, filling in the shape, which is then normalised to the range [−1, 1].

  3. Coarse alignment. An oriented bounding box gives the object’s centre (the mean of its points) and its rotation (the principal axes from PCA of the point covariance). Because this is still rough, rotation and scale are tuned by maximising the overlap (IoU), which gives the coarse alignment.

  4. Geometry-guided sparse attention. Reference point clouds are rendered from the query’s coarse pose. Normalised direction vectors between reference and query points build a top-K mask for cross-attention, with Gumbel-Softmax used for soft top-K sampling; pairs that fail to match are masked out, so attention concentrates on visible, relevant regions. A multi-scale fusion module weighs global against local features.

  5. Refine and select. Refine: the object scale and pose are optimised jointly: the pose by rendering the shape and minimising its projection error against the anchor image, and the scale by sampling scales within a range and choosing by IoU against the reconstructed shape. The relative pose to the query is then computed.

    Select: each pose hypothesis is rendered and compared with the query to give a feature vector; a self-attention module scores all hypotheses together, and top-K filtering selects the final pose.

Results

Mean ADD(-S) accuracy 83.2 % on LM, LMO and YCB-Video with four reference images and 0.9 s per object, against 75.8 % for FS6D + ICP, 70.1 % for LatentFusion (both with 16 references) and 76.5 % for Any6D (Table 1).
67.3 % on the heavily occluded LMO, against 58.6 %, 53.5 % and 57.9 % for the same three methods (Table 1).
On LMO, replacing the geometry-guided sparse attention with plain fully connected attention lowers accuracy to 64.5 % (Table 2).

The comparison uses three BOP benchmarks: LINEMOD (LM), Occlusion LINEMOD (LMO), where object visibility can drop below 40 %, and YCB-Video (YCBV). Accuracy is the ADD(-S) score at a threshold of 0.1 times the object diameter. Among the methods that do not use a CAD model, SFRF6D is the most accurate on all three datasets (92.1 %, 67.3 % and 90.2 %) and the fastest. FoundationPose, which uses the CAD model, remains more accurate, with a mean of 89.7 % at 1.0 s; the authors describe SFRF6D’s precision as slightly lower, in exchange for needing no CAD model and less computation.

The ablation on LMO (Table 2) separates the parts. Removing the view selector, which chooses among the rendered views, and using all of them keeps accuracy close (66.2 %) but raises the time from 0.94 s to 1.32 s. The number of references matters most at the low end: one reference gives 57.3 %, two give 63.4 %, four give 67.3 % and eight give 68.1 % at 1.03 s, so the authors settle on four as the balance between accuracy and cost. With a single reference the reconstructed shape depends heavily on that one view, and features cannot be aligned robustly when occlusion or the viewpoint difference is large. The authors list pretrained foundation models, dynamic multi-object scenes and lighter models for mobile and edge platforms as future work.

item.title: Volume Measurement Technology of Dispensing Transparent Adhesives Based on Line Laser Scanning
item.description:
The problem

Pneumatic dispensers meter adhesive through air pressure and valve opening time, and fluctuations in air pressure make the amount they deposit uneven. Too much adhesive overflows; too little gives weak bonding or poor airtightness. Measuring the volume of each dispensed bead provides the data needed to calibrate the discharge. For transparent adhesives, though, traditional optical 3D measurement methods show large errors or fail to reconstruct the bead completely.

A line-laser scanner works by locating a bright laser stripe in a camera image. On a transparent bead, part of the laser light travels into the adhesive and through it. That transmitted light causes internal scattering and reflection interference, which degrades the 3D reconstruction.

How it works

The method works on two levels. On the optical side, complementary spectral background optimization (CSBO) suppresses the transmitted light through the colour of the substrate alone. On the algorithmic side, an improved stripe-centre extractor collects several candidate points per image row and scores them, so that noise does not end up on the centre line. Geometry analysis then turns the reconstructed surface into a volume.

  1. Absorb the transmitted light (CSBO). A material absorbs light of one colour and shows the complementary colour, and green-yellow is the complementary colour of violet. The 3D sensor uses a violet laser, so the adhesive is dispensed onto a green-yellow substrate. The substrate absorbs the laser light that passes through the bead, which suppresses scattering and specular reflection without extra measurement tools or equipment.
  2. Find candidate regions in each row. After mean filtering, each pixel row of a stripe image is searched for candidate regions: a region starts where the grey level rises by at least a threshold K and ends where it falls by at least K. One row can contain several regions.
  3. One candidate centre per region. Within each region, a grey-scale centre of gravity with the weight w(I) = I / (256 − I) gives a candidate centre point; the weight emphasises the brightest pixels.
  4. Score and select (DWMF-SC). The dynamic weighted multi-factor scoring constraints method scores each candidate as 0.5 × continuity (how many points in the neighbouring rows lie within an offset threshold) + 0.1 × intensity + 0.4 × history (closeness to the point chosen in the previous row). Candidates darker than 10% of the row’s brightest candidate, or from regions wider than 20 pixels, score zero. The highest-scoring candidate is kept, one point per row.
  5. From centre lines to volume. All centre lines are projected into a depth map. A plane fitted by principal component analysis (PCA) to randomly sampled platform regions defines the datum, and a rigid-body transformation levels the depth map. 3D Otsu thresholding and eight-neighbourhood connectivity analysis segment the adhesive. Each pixel of the adhesive region then counts as a prism with base Δx × Δy and height z, so V = Δx·Δy·Σz.

Results

Average relative volume error 1.39% on the green-yellow substrate (maximum 1.55%), while the same method gives 9.05%, 8.03% and 8.63% on blue, pink and purple substrates (Table II, Fig. 13).
Continuous, smooth stripe centre lines on an image with strong surface roughness and edge diffusion noise, where the Steger and thinning methods pick up noise points and the gray-scale center of gravity method fails (Fig. 11).

For the volume experiment, a precision dispensing nozzle laid similar straight beads of transparent adhesive onto four substrates (green-yellow, blue, pink and purple), and each specimen was weighed on a precision electronic balance to obtain the reference value. Each specimen was scanned in a workshop environment and measured five times; the predicted weight is the measured volume times the adhesive density, 0.0011 g/mm³. On the green-yellow substrate the five relative errors range from 1.32% to 1.55%; on the other three substrates they range from 8.01% to 9.16%. The authors conclude that CSBO improves the 3D reconstruction accuracy of transparent adhesives.

The centre-line experiment uses a stripe image of a metallic part, where surface roughness makes the stripe profile uneven and the metallic lustre adds edge diffusion noise. The Steger method expects a Gaussian stripe profile and extracts multiple centre points near the noisy edges; the gray-scale center of gravity method, computed over the whole column, fails under the noise; and the thinning method extracts part of its skeleton from noise points. The proposed method follows the shape of the stripe with continuous, smooth centre points, which the authors attribute to the candidate points mechanism and the DWMF-SC selection.

item.title: SemReg: Semantics-Constrained Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, so that they can be merged into one. Recent learned methods describe every point by the shape around it, let the two scans exchange information through cross-attention, and then match points. Shape alone is often ambiguous, though: partial scans of a bed and a table can look geometrically alike. Cross-attention also lets every region of one scan interact with every region of the other, including pairs that are unlikely to overlap, such as a chair in one scan and a table in the other. These superfluous interactions lead to wrong matches.

Indoor scans captured with RGB-D cameras come with colour images, and semantic understanding is far more mature for 2D images than for 3D geometry. An earlier cross-modal method, PCR-CG, added image colour to the 3D features, but it uses only colour, not the semantic content of the images, and its features remain inconsistent.

How it works

SemReg is a 2D–3D cross-modal network. It keeps a standard 3D backbone for shape features and adds a semantic signal taken from the RGB frames, which it uses in three places: inside attention, at matching time, and in the training loss.

  1. Two scans with their colour frames. The input is a pair of partially overlapping point clouds, each with its RGB images. A KPConv backbone downsamples each cloud and extracts local shape features.
  2. Semantic features from the images. A pretrained DINOv2 network, kept frozen, extracts features from the RGB images. Using depth and the camera parameters, these are projected onto the 3D points and added to the shape features in self-attention.
  3. A semantic prior guides cross-attention. For each source point, SemReg finds the target points whose semantic features closely resemble its own and places a Gaussian over 3D distance around each one. The mixture of these Gaussians, the Gaussian Mixture Semantic Prior (GMSP), weights cross-attention so that features interact mainly between semantically similar regions.
  4. Matching within similar semantics. The Semantics Constrained Matching module sets the score of a candidate pair to zero when the semantic prior says the two points belong to unrelated regions. During training, a Semantics Aware Focal Loss supervises only pairs that are semantically related.
  5. Pose from the surviving matches. The final rotation and translation are estimated from the correspondences with RANSAC, and can be refined further with ICP.

Results

Registration recall 94.7 % on 3DMatch and 75.9 % on 3DLoMatch, the highest of all methods compared on both (Table 1).
95.4 % and 77.4 % after ICP refinement (Table 2).
Replacing all four semantic components (semantics constrained matching, semantics aware focal loss, semantic self-attention and GMSP-guided cross-attention) with standard counterparts drops recall to 92.1 % and 66.5 % (Table 3).

The evaluation uses 3DMatch, an indoor RGB-D benchmark, and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch (scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap). Registration recall is the share of scan pairs whose estimated transformation is accurate to within 0.2 m (RMSE). SemReg leads on both splits, ahead of SIRA-PCR on 3DMatch and GeoTransformer on 3DLoMatch, and in the paper’s ICP-refinement comparison its margin over the next-best method grows to 1.5 and 2.9 points. The semantic components matter most when overlap is small: they account for 9.4 points of recall on 3DLoMatch, against 2.6 points on 3DMatch. In one extreme case with 12.53 % overlap, where the only shared object is a chair, the semantic prior still locates the chair in the target scan and the registration succeeds, while GeoTransformer fails.

SemReg matches at a coarse level, with 0.1K–1K correspondences per pair against 6K–7K for dense methods such as GeoTransformer. Its inlier ratio (the share of correspondences within 0.1 m under the ground-truth transformation) is therefore lower than that of some competitors, although its registration recall is higher. Results on the outdoor KITTI dataset are reported in the supplementary material. The method needs RGB images aligned with the scan, so it does not apply directly to standalone point clouds; the authors suggest rendering images from the point cloud as a future workaround.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration estimates the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping scans. Most learned methods describe each point by its local geometry, match the descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC and solve for the transformation. Recent Transformer-based methods work on a sparse, sub-sampled set of points and let every sparse point attend to all the others, and some add the points’ relative positions so that attention knows where each point sits.

Sub-sampling throws away fine-grained structure, though, and relative position does not help when two sparse points are close to each other in space but far apart along the surface. The paper’s example is the top of a chair next to the corner of a desk: the two points have similar local geometry because they lie in the same neighbourhood, and their relative position barely separates them because they are close in Cartesian space. Their features become ambiguous and lead to wrong matches. In the dense point cloud the difference is easy to see, since the route from one to the other along the surface is long; in the sparse points it is hard to observe.

How it works

TopFormer follows a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline and adds one ingredient: a topological structure encoding that tells the Transformer how each pair of sparse points is connected along the surface. Because the sparse points are a subset of the dense points, this surface information can be measured on the dense cloud and handed to the sparse points, which the authors call a sparse-through-dense strategy.

  1. Close in space, far along the surface. A KPConv encoder extracts local features at a sparse and a dense level. Two sparse points such as a chair top and a desk corner can look alike to it, and their relative position does little to separate them.
  2. Sparse points inside the dense graph. Down-sampling uses furthest point sampling, so every sparse point is also a dense point. On the dense points, TopFormer builds a K-nearest-neighbour graph, keeping only edges shorter than a radius τ.
  3. Geodesic distance by shortest path. For two sparse points p and q, Dijkstra’s algorithm on the dense graph gives the geodesic distance from p to q, the length of the shortest route along the surface.
  4. Direction from normals, independent of their sign. Normals estimated by PCA are unoriented, and scans can be in arbitrary poses, so the normals are hard to re-orient consistently. TopFormer therefore uses the sines of the angle between the normal at p and the vector from p to q, and of the angle between the two normals; flipping a normal turns an angle α into π − α and leaves the sine unchanged.
  5. Encoding inside attention, then matching. The geodesic distance, the Euclidean distance and the two sines are mapped by a sinusoidal function into the topological structure encoding, which is added to the keys of self-attention. Cross-attention then lets the two clouds exchange information; sparse points are matched from a confidence matrix, the matches are refined at the dense level with an optimal transport layer, and RANSAC estimates the final rotation and translation.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) of 92.4 % on 3DMatch and 75.1 % on 3DLoMatch with 5,000 correspondences, against 92.0 % and 75.0 % for GeoTransformer (Table 1).
On KITTI, 99.8 % registration recall with a relative translation error of 6.7 cm, the lowest in the comparison (Table 2).
Removing the topological structure encoding lowers recall to 89.7 % and 67.4 % on 3DMatch and 3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The indoor experiments use 3DMatch and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch, which holds the scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m, computed with 50K RANSAC iterations. TopFormer’s registration recall is the highest, or tied for highest, at every correspondence number tested (5,000 down to 250) on both splits, and its feature matching recall on 3DMatch stays between 98.4 % and 98.7 %.

Its inlier ratio is below GeoTransformer’s at 5,000 correspondences (71.7 % against 71.9 % on 3DMatch, 37.2 % against 43.5 % on 3DLoMatch), but higher at smaller numbers, for example 82.8 % against 76.0 % on 3DMatch and 53.1 % against 46.2 % on 3DLoMatch at 1,000. On the outdoor KITTI odometry data, most of the compared methods already reach 99.8 % recall; TopFormer matches that, with a rotation error of 0.27°.

The ablation study shows that both parts of the encoding contribute. Without the geodesic distance, registration recall falls from 92.4 % to 90.3 % on 3DMatch and from 75.1 % to 72.3 % on 3DLoMatch; without the normal-based directional terms it falls to 91.9 % and 73.9 %. Dropping the encoding entirely, which leaves a vanilla Transformer, costs 2.7 and 7.7 points of recall, and the inlier ratio falls by 8.6 and 5.6 points.

item.title: WTAYOLO: A Detection Model for Weak Scratches on Metal Surfaces
item.description:
The problem

Scratches on the surface of lithium batteries significantly affect their electrochemical performance and operational safety, so stringent scratch detection is crucial for product quality. Detection remains difficult, however: lithium battery materials are reflective, and the morphology of the scratches themselves makes them hard for detection algorithms to pick up.

How it works

WTAYOLO is a detection model for weak scratches on metal surfaces. It combines photometric stereo imaging, which tackles the reflections, with a new module, WTAConv, which improves how scratch features are extracted from the images.

  1. Photometric stereo imaging. WTAYOLO uses a photometric stereo system, which reduces interference from surface reflections.
  2. A wider receptive field. The WTAConv module expands the receptive field, strengthening the extraction of scratch features from the images.
  3. Channel and spatial attention. Within WTAConv, channel and spatial attention mechanisms strengthen important features and suppress redundant information.
  4. Scratch detection. The model detects the subtle scratches.

Results

mAP50 of 86.8 %, a 5.1 % improvement over the YOLOv11n baseline, without increasing the number of parameters.

The authors conclude that the method strikes an effective balance between accuracy and model cost-effectiveness, providing an effective solution for industrial applications.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1145/3725949.3725956.

item.title: Weighted Point Cloud Normal Estimation
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners carry no normals and are often corrupted by noise, yet accurate normals help downstream tasks such as noise filtering and surface reconstruction. The classic approach, PCA, computes each point’s normal from the covariance of its neighbours; it is simple but tends to blur details and is fragile on noisy data. Learning-based regressors such as PCPNet and Nesti-Net are more robust to noise, but they ignore that neighbouring points contribute differently to the central point’s normal, which can make them inaccurate on complex surfaces. Surface-fitting methods such as DeepFit and AdaFit adapt well to complicated geometry but become less robust under severe noise.

How it works

The method regresses the normal of each point from a local patch around it, and it learns to weight the points of that patch by how relevant they are to the central point. Training has two stages: a contrastive pre-training stage that teaches the point encoder and weight regressor to relate patches to normals, and a normal estimation stage that fine-tunes them together with a normal regressor.

  1. A local patch. For each point, the patch contains its N nearest neighbours (N = 700 in the experiments). The patch is normalised to a unit sphere and aligned with a rotation R computed by PCA on the patch.
  2. Uniform weights fall short. Regressing the normal with every point weighted equally lets less relevant neighbours pull the estimate away from the true normal.
  3. Learned point weights. A point encoder built from DGCNN’s EdgeConv layers produces per-point features, and an MLP weight regressor predicts a weight for each point. The training target is the squared cosine between the central point’s ground-truth normal and each neighbour’s ground-truth normal, so points with similar normals count as more relevant. The weights multiply the features element-wise, F′ = W ⊙ F.
  4. Contrastive pre-training. A second branch encodes the central point’s ground-truth normal with MLPs. Both features pass through projection heads, and a temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss pulls each patch–normal pair together while pushing apart the other pairs in the batch. The weight loss is added to this loss.
  5. Weighted normal regression. The pre-trained encoder and weight regressor are fine-tuned with a normal regressor of fully connected layers, trained with a cosine loss plus the weight loss. The predicted normal is normalised and rotated back with R⁻¹.

Results

Average normal-angle RMSE 17.42° over the four noise levels of the PCPNet shapes with Gaussian noise, the lowest of all compared methods (AdaFit 17.66°, DeepFit 18.14°, best PCA setting 20.23°) (Table I).
Lowest error at the 0.60 %, 0.84 % and 1.20 % noise levels (noise as a share of the bounding-box diagonal), e.g. 21.48° vs 21.94° for AdaFit at 1.20 % (Table I).
On the PCPNet validation set, the full pipeline reaches 14.46°, against 21.15° for the baseline trained with the cosine loss alone (Table II).

The synthetic test set contains 19 PCPNet shapes, each with four Gaussian noise levels (0.36 %, 0.6 %, 0.84 % and 1.2 % of the bounding-box diagonal); the method is compared with PCA, the surface-fitting methods DI (Deep Iterative), DeepFit and AdaFit, and the regression methods PCPNet and Nesti-Net. At the lowest noise level DeepFit is slightly ahead (13.18° vs 13.25°); the method’s advantage appears as the noise grows. The ablation shows that both ideas matter: without the weight regression the error is 14.70°, and without the contrastive pre-training it is 18.21°.

On raw scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, compared against the clean normals the dataset provides, the method has lower error than AdaFit and Nesti-Net on the three shapes shown. On the Paris-rue-Madame street scans, where no ground truth exists, its normals are tidier on complex areas such as a window lattice while keeping features such as a building eave and a car light. Used as input to point cloud filtering, its normals give the best filtering result by Chamfer distance, and in Poisson reconstruction of a sharp Star shape they give a more accurate tip.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of moving object by double sampling based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high precision, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, and the 3D shape is computed from the phase of the deformed fringes and the system parameters. Because several images are needed, traditional PSP requires the object to stay static during reconstruction. Once it moves during fringe projection and capture, errors are introduced.

Earlier work tracks the object’s motion and compensates the resulting error, estimates the motion between the 3D data of adjacent frames, or uses a high-speed imaging system with shifted Gray code. One approach that estimates motion from the object’s start and end states is limited to uniform motion, and deep-learning methods that recover phase from a single fringe pattern need time-consuming network training and are hard to run in real time. The authors therefore look for a motion-error compensation method suited to real-time phase-shift measurement.

How it works

The method changes how the images are captured and how the phase is computed. The camera is triggered twice during every projected fringe pattern, so two images taken under the same fringe differ only by the object’s motion. With the motion known from tracking, a least-squares model recovers the object’s phase from three consecutive images, and overlapping groups of three images give one phase map each.

  1. Two shots per fringe. A trigger control device is added to the camera and projector. The projector projects N fringe images at a set rate and triggers the camera twice in each projection cycle: I11 and I12 are captured while fringe I1 is projected, I21 and I22 while I2 is projected, and so on.
  2. Separate motion from phase shift. Two images taken under the same projected fringe, such as I11 and I12, have no PSP phase shift between them (δ1 = 0), so they differ only by the object’s motion. Images taken under different fringes also carry the PSP phase shift δ2 = 2π/N. The three images I11, I12 and I21 are therefore analysed together.
  3. Track the motion. The rotation matrix and translation vector describing the object’s motion are obtained by tracking the object. From them follows the coordinate transformation (fn, gn) that relates each point’s position before and after the motion.
  4. Solve for the phase by least squares. Each of the three images is written as A + B cos(ϕ + δk) + C sin(ϕ + δk), where A, B and C are unknowns and ϕ is the reference-plane phase at the transformed coordinates. Minimising the squared error over the three images (N = 3) leads to a linear system D X = E for X = [A B C]T, and the phase change caused by the object is φ = tan−1(−C/B). The object is then reconstructed from the phase and the system parameters.
  5. Multiplex the images. Every three consecutive images give one object phase map, so the groups overlap and a new frame starts with each new image. Traditional PSP needs three projected patterns for each frame.

Results

Simulated object moving 10 pixels between fringe patterns: the proposed method reconstructs the block, while traditional PSP on the same images gives large errors (Figs. 5 and 6).
Two images per projected fringe, captured through a trigger control device on the camera and projector (Fig. 1).
One object phase map from every three consecutive images, by multiplexing the fringe images (Fig. 2).
Shooting frame rate twice the projector’s highest frame rate, because the camera shoots twice per fringe.

The method is verified by simulation. Fringe patterns are simulated for a static object and for an object that moves from left to right by 10 pixels between each two fringe patterns. For comparison, the static patterns are reconstructed with traditional PSP. In the moving case, images taken under the same projected fringe contain only the object’s motion, while images under different fringes contain both the fringe phase shift and the motion. The rotation matrix and translation vector of the motion are computed by tracking the object, the phase is computed with the proposed model, and with multiplexing every three images give an object phase map. These phase maps at different frames give a high-frame-rate 3D reconstruction of the moving block (Fig. 5). Traditional PSP applied to the same images shows large errors (Fig. 6).

In their conclusion, the authors note that the method only needs a newly derived formula and the projection of the first two fringe patterns of a three-step phase shift to reconstruct the moving object, and that it doubles the shooting frame rate at low cost without losing the advantages of PSP. The comparison with traditional PSP is shown visually in Figs. 5 and 6.

item.title: Parallel Curvature Filter for High Performance Image Processing
item.description:
The problem

The curvature filter smooths and denoises an image by implicitly reducing a curvature energy, such as Gaussian curvature, mean curvature or total variation. It treats the image as a surface and repeatedly applies a cheap local operator to every pixel, each pass lowering the regularisation energy. The filter is fast, but many images that need enhancing are high-resolution or must be processed in real or near-real time, and on a CPU a large image such as 2048 × 2048 still takes minutes.

The most expensive part of the filter is a set of eight convolutions over the image. Inspired by the way GPUs run the convolutions of convolutional neural networks, the authors parallelise these convolutions on the GPU.

How it works

Each iteration of the curvature filter enumerates eight candidate moves for every pixel, picks the smallest one and applies it. PCF computes the eight candidates for all pixels at once with convolution kernels on the GPU.

  1. The image as a surface. The image intensity U is interpreted as a surface over the pixel grid. The curvature regularisers all work on the local 3 × 3 neighbourhood around each pixel.
  2. Eight tangent-plane projections. A surface can be locally approximated by its tangent plane. In the 3 × 3 neighbourhood, eight tangent planes through neighbouring pixels are enumerated, giving eight projection distances d1 … d8 for the centre pixel.
  3. Eight convolutions on the GPU. Each distance is computed for every pixel at once as a convolution of the image. These eight convolutions are the most computationally expensive part of the algorithm; PCF runs them in CUDA and uses the GPU’s shared memory to accelerate them.
  4. Pick the smallest distance and update. For every pixel, the distance dm with the smallest magnitude is selected (ABSMIN) and added to the pixel: Ut+1 = Ut + dm. The smallest distance indicates the closest fit to the desired geometry and to the original image.
  5. Iterate. Repeating the update regularises the image surface step by step, which the paper shows by plotting the intensity along one line of the image after 10 and 30 iterations.

Results

33.2 gigapixels per second on a single GPU.
About 87 s on the CPU versus about 6 s on the GPU for 3,000 iterations on the same image (Fig. 3).

The CUDA implementation was run with GPU block sizes from 16 to 32 on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti (3,584 CUDA cores, 11,264 MB of global memory, 49,152 bytes of shared memory per block) and compared with the original curvature filter on an Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 CPU at 3.50 GHz. In Fig. 3 the computation time grows with the number of iterations on both, but far more slowly on the GPU. The authors conclude that this speed makes the filter suitable for real-time applications such as video processing and biomedical image processing.

The paper also applies Gaussian-curvature and mean-curvature versions of PCF to a photograph and plots the intensity along one line after 10 and 30 iterations. In both, the profile becomes smoother as iterations accumulate; judging from these profiles, the authors find the mean-curvature PCF more efficient at smoothing than the Gaussian-curvature PCF (a comparison of smoothing, not of running time).
